items.summary: Practical Use Cases for Data Pipelines in Detection Engineering Back in 2023, I wrote about why you need Data Engineering Pipelines before an enterprise SIEM . It opened with the classic “Data is the new oil” line and a simple question: why are so many detection engineers still dealing with log data in its crude form? Crude logs mean the dirty job of cleaning, parsing and enriching data lands on the desk of SIEM and content engineers. Over and over again, for every new detection use case. Three years later, most of the pipeline discussions out there still revolve around one thing: cost. Licensing, storage, GB/day. You know the drill. Money is always a valid driver. However, shortening detection delivery time and improving the overall quality of detection output are directly tied to costs too. This is a follow-up with a focus on practical use cases where refined data, delivered by a pipeline, speeds up the implementation of Threat Detection use cases. The pipeline is not where the alerting decision is made. It’s where the dirty job gets done, so detection engineers can focus on the detection logic and advanced use cases (alert frameworks, detection models, etc). TLDR: in case you landed here for the detection takeaways only, skip to the “Category 1 — Advanced Parsing” section below! From 2023 to 2026: what has changed? In the original article, the main point was about the (log) data lifecycle: ingestion, transformation and consumption. Traditional SIEM architectures handled that in a very rudimentary fashion. Log shippers sending data to a SIEM index as the final destination. That’s it. Very little work was done to polish the data before it hit the SIEM storage layer, shifting the data quality problem to SIEM and content engineers. After all, the cruder the log, the longer the time-to-value. Decoupling ingestion, filtering and enrichment from the SIEM was supposed to leave the platform with a clear primary role: Security Analytics. So, are we there yet? Partially. Data pipelines became a product category on their own, and the SIEM market is clearly adapting to them. This article is sponsored by Axoflow , full disclosure at the end of the article. The most popular argument for them today is breaking log lock-in. With a routing and transformation layer in front of the SIEM, switching SIEMs no longer means re-plumbing thousands of servers and hundreds of log source types from scratch. A common setup I see working in the field: detection and triage stay in the SIEM, while the pipeline sits in front of it, forking archival data to cheaper storage. Still, notice how most of the market discussion is about where data goes and how much it costs. Not about accelerating detection use case delivery by providing refined, enriched data instead of raw data. That’s the gap I want to explore here. The obvious Use Cases Before getting into threat detection, let’s get the well-known use cases out of the way. Those are the ones you will find in any vendor deck, so I’m not going to spend much time on them. Pipeline unification: replacing the accumulated sprawl of SIEM agents, cloud forwarders, endpoint collectors and scripts with one centrally managed pipeline. Declarative config, central routing policies, and one view of health, drops and volume. Log normalization: consistent field names, formats and values across sources, so detection queries stop compensating for messy data (remember the FourToSixMapping blind spot?). Routing & reduction: sending the right data to the right destination. Security-relevant events go to the SIEM, the bulky compliance stuff goes to cheaper storage, and debug noise goes nowhere. Now, to the fun part. Data Pipeline Use Cases for Detection Engineers Each stage below is one category of use cases that can be outsourced from the Analytics stage to the Data Pipeline one. By the time an event reaches the SIEM, it’s refined: normalized, parsed, enriched and labeled. The detection logic still lives in the SIEM, it just has much less dirty work to do. Category 1 — Advanced Parsing Every SIEM problem starts with a poorly designed use case. And many poorly designed use cases start with poorly prepared data. If the data is not ready for questioning, the detection engineer ends up preparing it at search time. Every single query. Every single time. URLs A URL is not a string. It’s a bundle of attributes. Scheme, subdomain, registered domain, top-level domain, path, file extension, query parameters. Each one is a detection opportunity on its own. When the URL lands in the SIEM as one long field, every detection that needs one of those parts must extract it again, usually with a regex that someone wrote years ago and nobody dares to touch. Parsing it upstream enables things like: Prevalence by registered domain instead of by full hostname only (attackers love disposable subdomains). Flagging encoded or unusually long query parameters. Spotting executable or script file extensions being downloaded, regardless of where they sit in the path. Base64 Flag / PowerShell Decoding If you’ve read my article on malicious encoded PowerShell , you know spotting the encoded command is just the beginning. The actual payload only reveals itself once it’s decoded. So why not decoding it before it hits the SIEM? Actually, that idea expands beyond PS command lines to any base64-encoded string. Imagine if you are able to write detections on base64-flagged commands only? The decoded payload can be stored right next to the original command line. From there: Analysts can search it like any other field during triage and hunting. Pattern-based indicators (more on that later) match against the actual content, not against a Base64 blob. Nobody needs to decode the same command again at search time. Pro Tip: never replace the original value, enrich it. Keep the raw command line intact, unless it's really rubbish data (static log descriptions, debugging info, etc). Besides forensics needs, decoding logic can fail, and when it does, you want the original to fall back to. Category 2 — External IP Enrichment In What makes up a solid SIEM query? , enrichment is one of the core query components. Back then, the advice was to perform lookups only after aggregation, to avoid looking up every single event. That’s still good advice. But what if the event arrives already enriched? External IP addresses are the perfect candidate here. Practically every detection involving remote access, authentication or C2 traffic depends on knowing a bit more about the other side of the connection. ASN The Autonomous System Number (ASN) tells you who owns the network an IP address belongs to: a residential ISP, a cloud provider, a hosting company or a VPN service. That’s a far more stable attribute than the IP address itself. Attackers rotate IPs all the time, but they often stick to the same hosting providers. And it opens the door to some great use cases: Once an incident is identified, the ASN is already available. Analysts, hunters, and responders can quickly use the SIEM to identify other IP addresses in the logs that belong to the same ASN. Detection and hunting queries can use the ASN as an anchor for filtering or aggregation, potentially providing better visibility and more effective ways to identify related activity. Geolocation In my SPL2 if command article , I showed how even vendor-enriched sources such as Entra ID sign-in logs don’t always come with a location value. Filling that gap at search time means paying for a lookup on every IP, every time the query runs. Do it at ingestion time, and it’s paid once. Axoflow : How to enrich an IP address and decode URL in the pipeline Another often-overlooked aspect is temporal accuracy : IP allocations and geolocation mappings can change over time, meaning search-time enrichment may apply today’s attributes to historical events rather than reflecting the context at the time they occurred. (Un)Known IP addresses This is one of the most valuable. Every organization owns or trusts a set of public network ranges: corporate egress IPs, VPN concentrators, cloud tenants, partner networks, scanners. Those usually live in a spreadsheet somewhere, or worse, hard-coded as exceptions across dozens of detection rules. What if that list (CIDR values in a JSON or CSV file) is maintained in one place and applied upstream? Every event containing a public IP address then carries a simple label: known or unknown. Or even better, the name of the known range. Now any detection can leverage that golden data point without a single hard-coded exception. Update the list once, and every rule downstream follows. This enrichment provides immediate context to distinguish traffic involving known organizational or trusted networks from communication with unknown IP ranges. Category 3 — Entity Prevalence By now you know I love baselines. If not, check Baselines 101 and Data Prevalence: The Game Changer . Quick recap: prevalence tells you how often something happens; a baseline uses those frequencies to define what’s normal. Today, most teams compute that at the SIEM layer through scheduled searches that maintain lookup tables or summary indexes. It works, but it’s yet another job to design, schedule and keep healthy. What if the pipeline does the remembering? First Time Seen The simplest form of prevalence is a binary one: have we seen this before? There are two ideas here: Enrich the log's entities with prevalence info (more expensive) Update Entity Prevalence tables or lookups (preferable) The idea is to have a pipeline that flags once it sees a relevant entity (file hash, domain, IP) for the first time (idea 1) or update a data store where an entity prevalence can be looked up from the SIEM (idea 2). That enables anomaly indicators to be used within your detection logic or models. I explore the concept in more details in the following article: Data Prevalence: The Game Changer in Threat Detection & IR Pro Tip: Rare does not mean alert-able. ⚠️ Not all rare or anomalous events are alert-able! ⚠️ A first-time-seen label is context, not a verdict. Its value shows up when combined with other signals, as part of a detection model, or during triage when the analyst asks “was this seen before?” That’s one of the most common questions during triage, by the way. Prevalence: The catch Keeping state is not free. A few things to consider before getting excited: Cold start: on day one, everything is new. The state needs a learning period before the labels mean anything. Time window: how long does an entity stay “known”? That’s the Circadian Window discussion again, now applied to the pipeline. Distributed state: pipelines scale horizontally. If two workers process events from the same entity, they need to share the same memory. Cardinality: remembering every command line ever seen is a bad idea. Pick entities with reasonable cardinality. Notice something? A pipeline that remembers entities over time is starting to do something a SIEM is supposed to do. Hold that thought, we’ll come back to it. Category 4 — Alert Signaling This is where things get really interesting from a detection engineering standpoint. If the pipeline can parse, enrich and remember, it can also flag. Not a full-blown security alert, but an alert signal . IOC matching Automated IOC matching is a must-have, as I suggest a framework here . Nobody should be manually scanning logs for indicators from the latest CTI report. Matching at the pipeline means every event is checked as it flows, no scheduled searches scanning the same data over and over again. But here’s the limitation: a pipeline typically sees what’s flowing now. When a new IOC arrives today, the events from last month have already passed through. So stream matching doesn’t replace IOC retro-hunting. It complements it. Fresh events get matched in the stream; historical data gets swept at the SIEM or the data lake. Detection Model Indicators Labeling If you follow this blog, you know I keep saying atomic alerts sent straight to the SOC queue are a recipe for alert fatigue (or fat AI bills). The strongest signal shows up only after collecting and scoring multiple indicators, aggregating them by an alert entity (usually the target or the origin of the attack). Now, those indicators need to come from somewhere. Many of them are simple, pattern-based, atomic observations. Picking on suspicious PowerShell one-liners, for example, the presence of any of the following already raises a red flag: A double encoded payload. A download cradle pattern. A common obfuscation pattern. Each of those is a perfect candidate for labeling at the pipeline. The event gets tagged with the indicators it matches, and the detection model at the SIEM does what it’s good at: aggregating, scoring and deciding whether to alert or not. That’s precisely the idea behind the indicators in PowerShell.Exposed : an indicator is not a detection on its own, it’s input for one. The benefits: Write once, consume many: the same label feeds multiple detection models, hunting queries and dashboards. Searchable signals: analysts and hunters can pivot on labels instead of rewriting regexes. Lighter detections: the heavy pattern matching is done before the data is stored, not every time a detection runs. Pro Tip: treat pipeline labeling logic as detection content. Version it, peer-review it and test it, just like any other Detection-as-Code artifact. The Controversial Part: Who Is Eating Whom? Go back and look at Categories 3 and 4. Keeping state about entities over time, matching IOCs, labeling events with detection indicators. Is that still a pipeline? Or is it a SIEM in disguise? Are pipelines becoming SIEMs? The pipeline products are clearly moving up the stack. Search, storage, enrichment, even some sort of detection. From where they sit, it makes sense: they already see all the data. We’ve seen this movie before. Many products that promised to replace the SIEM ended up rebuilding SIEM features once they hit production. So that’s a move worth watching more closely over the coming years. Or are SIEMs absorbing pipelines? On the other side, SIEM vendors are adding native pipeline capabilities: filtering, routing, transformation and enrichment at ingestion time, sometimes even before the data leaves the customer’s network. And it’s not only the incumbents. New SIEM products are being designed with the pipeline built in from day one, not as an add-on. In the long run, pipeline features look like a checkbox in the SIEM feature list. A very important checkbox, but a checkbox nonetheless. But to be fair, there’s a strong argument for keeping the pipeline independent: leverage. The main reason pipelines broke log lock-in is that they sit outside the SIEM. If your SIEM vendor owns your pipeline too, the lock-in is back, just one layer earlier. So it’s a trade-off, as always. Convenience and tighter integration versus independence and negotiation power. Which side are you on? Closing Thoughts In 2023, the message was: you need data pipelines before an enterprise SIEM. In 2026, I’d add: stop treating them as plumbing only. A pipeline is where the dirty job gets outsourced. Data reaches the SIEM normalized, parsed, enriched and labeled, refined instead of crude, and detection engineers spend their time on detection logic, not on data preparation. Cost reduction is a great way to get the budget approved. Faster delivery of detection use cases is where the real return is. And whether the pipeline ends up inside the SIEM or the other way around, one thing doesn’t change: the less time spent cleaning crude data, the more time spent actually detecting threats. Practical Use Cases for Data Pipelines in Detection Engineering

Crude logs mean the dirty job of cleaning, parsing and enriching data lands on the desk of SIEM and content engineers. Over and over again, for every new detection use case.

Three years later, most of the pipeline discussions out there still revolve around one thing: cost. Licensing, storage, GB/day. You know the drill.

Money is always a valid driver. However, shortening detection delivery time and improving the overall quality of detection output are directly tied to costs too.

This is a follow-up with a focus on practical use cases where refined data, delivered by a pipeline, speeds up the implementation of Threat Detection use cases.

The pipeline is not where the alerting decision is made. It’s where the dirty job gets done, so detection engineers can focus on the detection logic and advanced use cases (alert frameworks, detection models, etc).

TLDR: in case you landed here for the detection takeaways only, skip to the “Category 1 — Advanced Parsing” section below!

From 2023 to 2026: what has changed?

In the original article, the main point was about the (log) data lifecycle: ingestion, transformation and consumption.

Very little work was done to polish the data before it hit the SIEM storage layer, shifting the data quality problem to SIEM and content engineers. After all, the cruder the log, the longer the time-to-value.

Decoupling ingestion, filtering and enrichment from the SIEM was supposed to leave the platform with a clear primary role: Security Analytics.

So, are we there yet?

Partially. Data pipelines became a product category on their own, and the SIEM market is clearly adapting to them.

The most popular argument for them today is breaking log lock-in. With a routing and transformation layer in front of the SIEM, switching SIEMs no longer means re-plumbing thousands of servers and hundreds of log source types from scratch.

A common setup I see working in the field: detection and triage stay in the SIEM, while the pipeline sits in front of it, forking archival data to cheaper storage.

Still, notice how most of the market discussion is about where data goes and how much it costs. Not about accelerating detection use case delivery by providing refined, enriched data instead of raw data.

That’s the gap I want to explore here.

The obvious Use Cases

Before getting into threat detection, let’s get the well-known use cases out of the way. Those are the ones you will find in any vendor deck, so I’m not going to spend much time on them.

  • Pipeline unification: replacing the accumulated sprawl of SIEM agents, cloud forwarders, endpoint collectors and scripts with one centrally managed pipeline. Declarative config, central routing policies, and one view of health, drops and volume.
  • Log normalization: consistent field names, formats and values across sources, so detection queries stop compensating for messy data (remember the FourToSixMapping blind spot?).
  • Routing & reduction: sending the right data to the right destination. Security-relevant events go to the SIEM, the bulky compliance stuff goes to cheaper storage, and debug noise goes nowhere.

Now, to the fun part.

Data Pipeline Use Cases for Detection Engineers

Each stage below is one category of use cases that can be outsourced from the Analytics stage to the Data Pipeline one.

By the time an event reaches the SIEM, it’s refined: normalized, parsed, enriched and labeled. The detection logic still lives in the SIEM, it just has much less dirty work to do.

Category 1 — Advanced Parsing

Every SIEM problem starts with a poorly designed use case. And many poorly designed use cases start with poorly prepared data.

If the data is not ready for questioning, the detection engineer ends up preparing it at search time. Every single query. Every single time.

URLs

A URL is not a string. It’s a bundle of attributes.

Scheme, subdomain, registered domain, top-level domain, path, file extension, query parameters. Each one is a detection opportunity on its own.

When the URL lands in the SIEM as one long field, every detection that needs one of those parts must extract it again, usually with a regex that someone wrote years ago and nobody dares to touch.

Parsing it upstream enables things like:

  • Prevalence by registered domain instead of by full hostname only (attackers love disposable subdomains).
  • Flagging encoded or unusually long query parameters.
  • Spotting executable or script file extensions being downloaded, regardless of where they sit in the path.
Base64 Flag / PowerShell Decoding

If you’ve read my article on malicious encoded PowerShell, you know spotting the encoded command is just the beginning. The actual payload only reveals itself once it’s decoded.

So why not decoding it before it hits the SIEM? Actually, that idea expands beyond PS command lines to any base64-encoded string. Imagine if you are able to write detections on base64-flagged commands only?

The decoded payload can be stored right next to the original command line. From there:

  • Analysts can search it like any other field during triage and hunting.
  • Pattern-based indicators (more on that later) match against the actual content, not against a Base64 blob.
  • Nobody needs to decode the same command again at search time.

Pro Tip: never replace the original value, enrich it. Keep the raw command line intact, unless it's really rubbish data (static log descriptions, debugging info, etc). Besides forensics needs, decoding logic can fail, and when it does, you want the original to fall back to.

Category 2 — External IP Enrichment

In What makes up a solid SIEM query?, enrichment is one of the core query components. Back then, the advice was to perform lookups only after aggregation, to avoid looking up every single event.

That’s still good advice. But what if the event arrives already enriched?

External IP addresses are the perfect candidate here. Practically every detection involving remote access, authentication or C2 traffic depends on knowing a bit more about the other side of the connection.

ASN

The Autonomous System Number (ASN) tells you who owns the network an IP address belongs to: a residential ISP, a cloud provider, a hosting company or a VPN service.

That’s a far more stable attribute than the IP address itself. Attackers rotate IPs all the time, but they often stick to the same hosting providers.

And it opens the door to some great use cases:

  1. Once an incident is identified, the ASN is already available. Analysts, hunters, and responders can quickly use the SIEM to identify other IP addresses in the logs that belong to the same ASN.
  2. Detection and hunting queries can use the ASN as an anchor for filtering or aggregation, potentially providing better visibility and more effective ways to identify related activity.
Geolocation

In my SPL2 if command article, I showed how even vendor-enriched sources such as Entra ID sign-in logs don’t always come with a location value. Filling that gap at search time means paying for a lookup on every IP, every time the query runs.

Do it at ingestion time, and it’s paid once.

Another often-overlooked aspect is temporal accuracy: IP allocations and geolocation mappings can change over time, meaning search-time enrichment may apply today’s attributes to historical events rather than reflecting the context at the time they occurred.

(Un)Known IP addresses

This is one of the most valuable.

Every organization owns or trusts a set of public network ranges: corporate egress IPs, VPN concentrators, cloud tenants, partner networks, scanners. Those usually live in a spreadsheet somewhere, or worse, hard-coded as exceptions across dozens of detection rules.

What if that list (CIDR values in a JSON or CSV file) is maintained in one place and applied upstream?

Every event containing a public IP address then carries a simple label: known or unknown. Or even better, the name of the known range.

Now any detection can leverage that golden data point without a single hard-coded exception. Update the list once, and every rule downstream follows.

This enrichment provides immediate context to distinguish traffic involving known organizational or trusted networks from communication with unknown IP ranges.

Category 3 — Entity Prevalence

By now you know I love baselines. If not, check Baselines 101 and Data Prevalence: The Game Changer.

Quick recap: prevalence tells you how often something happens; a baseline uses those frequencies to define what’s normal.

Today, most teams compute that at the SIEM layer through scheduled searches that maintain lookup tables or summary indexes. It works, but it’s yet another job to design, schedule and keep healthy.

What if the pipeline does the remembering?

First Time Seen

The simplest form of prevalence is a binary one: have we seen this before?

There are two ideas here:

  1. Enrich the log's entities with prevalence info (more expensive)
  2. Update Entity Prevalence tables or lookups (preferable)

The idea is to have a pipeline that flags once it sees a relevant entity (file hash, domain, IP) for the first time (idea 1) or update a data store where an entity prevalence can be looked up from the SIEM (idea 2).

That enables anomaly indicators to be used within your detection logic or models. I explore the concept in more details in the following article:

Data Prevalence: The Game Changer in Threat Detection & IR

Pro Tip: Rare does not mean alert-able.

⚠️ Not all rare or anomalous events are alert-able! ⚠️

A first-time-seen label is context, not a verdict. Its value shows up when combined with other signals, as part of a detection model, or during triage when the analyst asks “was this seen before?”

That’s one of the most common questions during triage, by the way.

Prevalence: The catch

Keeping state is not free. A few things to consider before getting excited:

  • Cold start: on day one, everything is new. The state needs a learning period before the labels mean anything.
  • Time window: how long does an entity stay “known”? That’s the Circadian Window discussion again, now applied to the pipeline.
  • Distributed state: pipelines scale horizontally. If two workers process events from the same entity, they need to share the same memory.
  • Cardinality: remembering every command line ever seen is a bad idea. Pick entities with reasonable cardinality.

Notice something? A pipeline that remembers entities over time is starting to do something a SIEM is supposed to do. Hold that thought, we’ll come back to it.

Category 4 — Alert Signaling

This is where things get really interesting from a detection engineering standpoint.

If the pipeline can parse, enrich and remember, it can also flag. Not a full-blown security alert, but an alert signal.

IOC matching

Automated IOC matching is a must-have, as I suggest a framework here. Nobody should be manually scanning logs for indicators from the latest CTI report.

Matching at the pipeline means every event is checked as it flows, no scheduled searches scanning the same data over and over again.

But here’s the limitation: a pipeline typically sees what’s flowing now. When a new IOC arrives today, the events from last month have already passed through.

So stream matching doesn’t replace IOC retro-hunting. It complements it. Fresh events get matched in the stream; historical data gets swept at the SIEM or the data lake.

Detection Model Indicators Labeling

If you follow this blog, you know I keep saying atomic alerts sent straight to the SOC queue are a recipe for alert fatigue (or fat AI bills).

The strongest signal shows up only after collecting and scoring multiple indicators, aggregating them by an alert entity (usually the target or the origin of the attack).

Now, those indicators need to come from somewhere.

Many of them are simple, pattern-based, atomic observations. Picking on suspicious PowerShell one-liners, for example, the presence of any of the following already raises a red flag:

  • A double encoded payload.
  • A download cradle pattern.
  • A common obfuscation pattern.
Each of those is a perfect candidate for labeling at the pipeline.

The event gets tagged with the indicators it matches, and the detection model at the SIEM does what it’s good at: aggregating, scoring and deciding whether to alert or not.

That’s precisely the idea behind the indicators in PowerShell.Exposed: an indicator is not a detection on its own, it’s input for one.

The benefits:

  • Write once, consume many: the same label feeds multiple detection models, hunting queries and dashboards.
  • Searchable signals: analysts and hunters can pivot on labels instead of rewriting regexes.
  • Lighter detections: the heavy pattern matching is done before the data is stored, not every time a detection runs.

Pro Tip: treat pipeline labeling logic as detection content. Version it, peer-review it and test it, just like any other Detection-as-Code artifact.

The Controversial Part: Who Is Eating Whom?

Go back and look at Categories 3 and 4. Keeping state about entities over time, matching IOCs, labeling events with detection indicators.

Is that still a pipeline? Or is it a SIEM in disguise?

Are pipelines becoming SIEMs?

The pipeline products are clearly moving up the stack. Search, storage, enrichment, even some sort of detection. From where they sit, it makes sense: they already see all the data.

We’ve seen this movie before. Many products that promised to replace the SIEM ended up rebuilding SIEM features once they hit production.

So that’s a move worth watching more closely over the coming years.

Or are SIEMs absorbing pipelines?

On the other side, SIEM vendors are adding native pipeline capabilities: filtering, routing, transformation and enrichment at ingestion time, sometimes even before the data leaves the customer’s network.

And it’s not only the incumbents. New SIEM products are being designed with the pipeline built in from day one, not as an add-on.

In the long run, pipeline features look like a checkbox in the SIEM feature list. A very important checkbox, but a checkbox nonetheless.

But to be fair, there’s a strong argument for keeping the pipeline independent: leverage.

The main reason pipelines broke log lock-in is that they sit outside the SIEM. If your SIEM vendor owns your pipeline too, the lock-in is back, just one layer earlier.

So it’s a trade-off, as always. Convenience and tighter integration versus independence and negotiation power.

Which side are you on?

Closing Thoughts

In 2023, the message was: you need data pipelines before an enterprise SIEM.

In 2026, I’d add: stop treating them as plumbing only.

A pipeline is where the dirty job gets outsourced. Data reaches the SIEM normalized, parsed, enriched and labeled, refined instead of crude, and detection engineers spend their time on detection logic, not on data preparation.

Cost reduction is a great way to get the budget approved. Faster delivery of detection use cases is where the real return is.

And whether the pipeline ends up inside the SIEM or the other way around, one thing doesn’t change: the less time spent cleaning crude data, the more time spent actually detecting threats.

items.title: Google Reveals How Russian Hackers Used One Cloud Breach to Compromise Another US Organization
items.summary: Russian state-sponsored hackers broke into a U.S. organization’s Google Workspace environment in late 2025, stole its staff directory and cloud files, and used information from the breach to target a second U.S. organization in 2026. Google and Mandiant said the hackers posed as an employee of the first victim, turning a familiar professional identity into a way to steal cloud credentials from the second. Neither organization was named. In its November 17 case study, Google identified the group as COLD RELIC, previously tracked as COLDRIVER and also known as Star Blizzard or Callisto. The U.S. Justice Department has tied Callisto to Russia’s Federal Security Service, or FSB. Google’s researchers said they saw evidence of fresh phishing activity as recently as November 2026. Google Cloud researchers previously identified the group’s LOSTKEYS document theft malware in a separate 2025 campaign. The new report does not identify a malware payload in either U.S. breach. Instead, it shows how stolen credentials, unauthorized authentication methods, and convincing impersonation were enough to steal cloud files and reach another organization. Google Reveals How Russian Hackers Used One Cloud Breach The first intrusion began with stolen credentials for a Google Workspace Super Admin account. The attackers sent repeated multi-factor authentication (MFA) prompts until the user approved one, a tactic known as MFA fatigue. They signed in through a residential proxy near the victim, making the connection look geographically routine. Once inside, they registered a device model the organization had not seen before. With administrator access, the group downloaded the organization’s entire cloud drive, both by retrieving files directly and by sharing them with an attacker-controlled email account. The hackers also exported the staff directory, started a tenant-wide Google Workspace Customer Takeout export, and deleted security alerts. Some attacker-enrolled passkeys remained usable after password and session resets because responders had not revoked the passkeys themselves. Google and Mandiant said the hackers posed as an employee of the first victim, turning a familiar professional identity into a way to steal cloud credentials from the second. Neither organization was named.

In its November 17 case study, Google identified the group as COLD RELIC, previously tracked as COLDRIVER and also known as Star Blizzard or Callisto.

The U.S. Justice Department has tied Callisto to Russia’s Federal Security Service, or FSB. Google’s researchers said they saw evidence of fresh phishing activity as recently as November 2026.

Google Cloud researchers previously identified the group’s LOSTKEYS document theft malware in a separate 2025 campaign. The new report does not identify a malware payload in either U.S. breach.

Instead, it shows how stolen credentials, unauthorized authentication methods, and convincing impersonation were enough to steal cloud files and reach another organization.

Google Reveals How Russian Hackers Used One Cloud Breach

items.title: Critical Apache HTTP Server RCE Vulnerability Actively Exploited in Attacks
items.summary: Apache’s HTTP/2 module, mod_http2, has a critical flaw tracked as CVE-2026-119618 that reportedly allows unauthenticated remote code execution. Apache released version 2.4.71 on November 11 to fix the flaw, which it rates as critical, while Singapore’s CSA assigns it a high-severity CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1/10. Singapore’s CSA warned of active exploitation on November 17, 2026, urging administrators to patch immediately. It also noted that a public PoC was available but provided no details about victims or attack scale. Wiz Research had reported no known exploitation when it published its analysis on November 11. The later alert changes the urgency for administrators who have not yet applied the update. The bug sits in assign_headers(), a function in the module that handles HTTP/2 traffic. Apache says the function does not properly control how multiple threads access a shared resource. This creates a race condition, meaning the result depends on which task gets to the resource first. The bug can corrupt the heap, an area of memory the server uses while it runs. Apache HTTP Server RCE Exploitation A successful attack can turn that memory corruption into remote code execution (RCE), allowing an attacker to run commands with the web server process’s permissions. Apache credited Anthropic’s OSS Scanner, which reported the issue on October 26, and Google Cloud researchers Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell, who reported it independently on November 3. Cybersecurity News previously covered the Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 patch and a separate Apache HTTP/2 code execution flaw fixed in May. The earlier fix does not protect servers from this vulnerability. The Apache security advisory lists versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 as affected when mod_http2 is enabled. It also lists standalone mod_h2 releases 2.0.8 through 2.0.42 as affected, including 2.0.42 itself. Servers configured to serve only HTTP/1.1 are not exposed to this flaw. Administrators should check the server’s active protocol settings rather than relying on the version number alone. Wiz found that 64% of the cloud environments it examined had resources running affected versions, while 51% had publicly exposed instances. Those figures do not account for whether HTTP/2 was enabled. They show where teams should check first, not how many environments could be exploited or how many were breached. Administrators should install Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 or later, or apply a package their operating system vendor confirms contains the fix. If an update must wait, temporarily disable HTTP/2 by setting Protocols http/1.1 and checking that individual virtual hosts do not still allow h2 or h2c. After reloading the service, verify that the affected Apache listeners no longer accept HTTP/2. Start with internet-facing servers, but include internal deployments in the patch plan. For systems that were exposed before the update, keep relevant logs and review them for signs of compromise. Installing the fix closes the vulnerability, but it cannot tell you whether someone exploited it before the upgrade. items.title: Flipper Devices Launches Flipper One Linux-based Multi-tool With Advanced Network Security Tools
items.summary: Flipper Devices has launched a Kickstarter campaign for Flipper One, a portable Linux computer built for network testing, hardware projects, and security research. Backing starts at $399, with shipping estimated for July 2027. The campaign runs from November 17 through December 17, 2026, making this a crowdfunding launch rather than immediate retail availability. The device combines Wi-Fi 6E, two Gigabit Ethernet ports, and an expansion system for cellular modems, software-defined radios, and storage. Its main appeal is bringing several network tools into one standalone unit, giving researchers a portable platform for checking networks and building custom testing setups. Flipper One Linux Multi-tool Flipper One is not a replacement for Flipper Zero. Zero focuses on NFC, RFID, infrared, sub-GHz radio, and other direct hardware links. One targets IP networks and Linux applications. As covered in our earlier Flipper One report , the two products serve different tasks rather than forming a simple upgrade path. Flipper One Feature Comparison (Image Source: Kickstarter) Flipper One supports up to five network uplinks, with options for routing, failover, load balancing, firewall rules, and VPN tunnels. It can act as both a Wi-Fi client and hotspot. Two independent 1 Gbps Ethernet ports also let users place it between wired devices as a transparent bridge or traffic sensor. Its network scanner is designed to discover active hosts, identify open ports and services, and map network layouts. Flipper also describes passive monitoring that can detect network attacks and report unusual activity. These functions could help administrators find exposed services and investigate traffic, although their real value will depend on software quality and testing. According to the official product page , its MediaTek wireless hardware supports Wi-Fi 6E across the 2.4, 5, and 6 GHz bands, with monitor mode support. Flipper is still testing advanced wireless features. Packet injection appears among its development goals, so buyers should not treat every planned Wi-Fi testing function as finished. An eight-core Rockchip RK3576 processor runs Linux, user applications, and high-speed interfaces. A separate Raspberry Pi RP2350 microcontroller handles the screen, buttons, battery, power states, and boot control. The firmware documentation explains this split, which keeps core device controls separate from the Linux system. That separation matters when a custom Linux build fails or the main processor is switched off. Users retain access to the built-in interface instead of depending entirely on a working operating system. Flipper also supports charging and SSH access through one USB-C cable, while desktop mode combines display output, power, and USB peripherals through a compatible connection. Flipper One Desktop Mode (Image Source: Kickstarter) Flipper is working with Collabora to bring the RK3576 platform into mainline Linux. This approach aims to reduce reliance on vendor-specific board support packages that can become difficult to maintain. For researchers, upstream support offers a clearer path to kernel updates, code review, and custom builds without maintaining large private patches. However, the open-source claims need context. In its May development update , Collabora said a proprietary DDR training component remained in the boot chain. Hardware video decoding and the AI accelerator were also unfinished. Those findings describe development status at that time, not proof that every limitation remains today. The internal M.2 slot supports PCIe, USB, and SATA connections for compatible modems, radios, and SSDs. A 5G modem is required to use the built-in eSIM for cellular data. GPIO accessories offer another route for custom hardware. This extends the community-driven approach seen in Flipper Zero firmware development , but on a different computing platform. For security teams, Flipper One promises a compact network lab rather than an automatic hacking device. Buyers should separate announced features from tested performance and treat the delivery date as an estimate. Its strongest potential lies in combining open Linux software, wired traffic analysis, wireless monitoring, and expandable hardware in one field-ready design. items.title: Microsoft’s Agent Framework PyPI Package Hacked to Steal Azure and GitHub Credentials
items.summary: Hackers published two malicious versions of Microsoft’s agent-framework package on the Python Package Index (PyPI) on November 17, 2026. Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 contained a credential stealer that could run during normal Python startup, even if an application never imported Agent Framework. The malware targeted Azure identities, GitHub credentials, and secrets used in automated builds. Wiz traced the first upload to 20:35 UTC and the second to about 21:08 UTC. Both versions were no longer available on PyPI by 21:30 UTC. Wiz identified 1.26.0 as the latest known clean release and put normal package traffic at about 41,000 downloads per week. It indicates the package’s overall use, not downloads of the malicious versions or the number of victims. Microsoft’s Agent Framework PyPI Compromised Both releases placed a .pth file in site-packages , the directory where Python stores installed libraries. Python processes these files during normal startup and can run executable lines in them. That meant an unrelated Python script could trigger the stealer simply by running in the affected environment. Cyber Security News documented a similar startup mechanism in its coverage of the elementary-data PyPI compromise . The two versions left different files behind. Version 1.26.1 used agent_framework_meta.pth and a collector named _telemetry.py . Version 1.26.2 restored the package’s original initializer and moved the malicious code into af_runtime_diag.py , triggered by af_runtime_diag.pth . A check limited to the first release’s files could therefore miss the second, even though both ran in the background and sent data to the same destination. Researchers found the malicious releases under the legitimate Microsoft-associated PyPI publisher, not under a lookalike name. Wiz found no matching python-1.26.1 tag or release in Microsoft’s GitHub repository and no malicious code on its main branch. The first malicious release also appeared only as a wheel, a ready-to-install Python package, rather than alongside a source archive and a matching agent-framework-core release. Those differences suggest it may have bypassed the usual build process, but the entry point remains unconfirmed Azure and GitHub Actions Credentials Socket’s analysis found that both versions searched environment variables, readable process data and local files for secrets. Targets included Azure CLI data, Azure DevOps agent credentials, Git credential stores, Docker and npm configuration, and application .env files. The stealer also tried to obtain fresh Azure managed identity and Azure DevOps tokens instead of relying only on credentials already stored on the system. Version 1.26.2 added requests for GitHub Actions OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens in workflows that could issue them. OIDC lets a build job prove its identity without storing a cloud password. If Microsoft Entra ID trusts that workflow, a stolen token could be exchanged for Azure access within the permissions granted to that identity. An earlier Microsoft durabletask supply chain incident also targeted build and cloud credentials, but Wiz has not linked the two attacks. Both versions sent compressed, encoded data to a specific webhook[.]site address. Wiz said the destination used the service’s free tier and that no more than 50 requests were captured. That is not a count of affected systems or exposed credentials. A single accepted request could contain several working secrets, including cloud tokens and package registry credentials. Search dependency lockfiles, build logs, Python environments, container images, and package caches for either version. If you find one, isolate the affected host or runner and avoid starting Python in that environment to inspect it. Check proxy logs for the specific webhook path listed in Socket’s indicators. Then rebuild from a known-good image or dependency set and pin agent-framework to 1.26.0. Removal from PyPI does not remove copies already installed or cached. From a clean system, revoke or rotate credentials that were available to the affected environment. Review Azure sign-in and activity logs for unexpected use of managed identities and service connections. For GitHub Actions jobs that installed 1.26.2 with id-token: write , check the Entra ID trust settings and sign-ins for the linked application. items.title: Critical Java4Shell Flaw Lets Hackers Execute Code Without Authentication on OpenJDK Servers
items.summary: A critical flaw in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder can let a remote attacker run code on an affected server without signing in. The vulnerability, dubbed Java4Shell and tracked as CVE-2026-114938, can also crash the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) or expose sensitive data held in its memory. Oracle released security updates on November 17, 2026, and the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) urged organizations to patch immediately. The flaw sits in HotSpot, the JVM that runs Java applications in many OpenJDK distributions. That differs from Log4Shell , which affected the Log4j logging library. Updating an application’s Java libraries will not replace a vulnerable runtime. Administrators need to identify the Java build each service actually runs, including any copy shipped by the application vendor. Security firm Calif rated Java4Shell 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, which puts it in the critical range. OpenJDK’s advisory lists a score of 8.1 under CVSS 3.1. The scores use different versions of the severity standard. Both describe a serious flaw, but neither means every Java server can be exploited. Exposure depends on the runtime, the processor, and how the application handles outside data. Calif researcher, Quang Luong, found the flaw while examining OpenJDK HotSpot with help from an AI coding tool. The disclosure follows Calif’s work on PHP2Shell and the emergency PHP patches . Both investigations found memory flaws in shared runtimes, but the PHP flaws and Java4Shell have different causes and require separate fixes. Base64 represents binary data as text so applications can pass it through systems that expect text. It is common in sign-in flows, file uploads, and network messages. On supported processors, HotSpot uses a faster decoder that handles several bytes at once. A mistake in that code can make the decoder write past the end of its allocated buffer before Java rejects the bad input. Rejecting it does not undo the memory damage. Java4Shell Exposes Java Applications Calif reported remote code execution without a login in default test setups of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira and Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate. Its tests against Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker required authentication. The researchers also demonstrated code execution in sample applications built with Apache Struts and Spring Boot. These results describe the setups Calif tested, not every installation of those products. The risk is not limited to servers that accept incoming requests. Calif also reported a client-side demonstration in which a Java program could be compromised after opening an encrypted TLS connection to a malicious server. The researchers compared the memory exposure to Heartbleed because a successful attack could reveal data already held by the process, such as session tokens or private keys. The two flaws do not share the same cause. The vulnerable decoder requires an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI support, a feature available on some Intel Xeon and newer AMD processors. ARM64 systems are not affected by this code path. The earlier Cybersecurity News report on the Java 17 flaw focused on that release line. The OpenJDK advisory now identifies fixes for Java 17, 21, 25 and 27. Oracle also lists a specific Java 8 Enterprise Performance Pack build and certain GraalVM builds as affected. There is no single exploit that works across all Java applications, according to Calif. WatchTowr also expects attacks to be tailored to individual products because the CPU, JDK, and the way the application uses Base64 all matter. The research demonstrations establish that code execution is possible, but they are not evidence of attacks against production systems. How to patch Java4Shell and Fix Versions Oracle’s fixed Java SE releases include 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1. Organizations using Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Azul Zulu, or another distribution should check their vendor’s advisory for the build that fixes this CVE. Product Affected build listed for this CVE Patched build or upgrade guidance Oracle Java SE 17 17.0.21.0.3 17.0.21.1 Oracle Java SE 21 21.0.13.0.3 21.0.13.1 Oracle Java SE 25 25.0.5.0.3 25.0.5.1 Oracle Java SE 27 27.0.1.0.3 27.0.1.1 Oracle Java 8 Enterprise Performance Pack 8u511b33-perf Install Oracle’s November 17 security update for the Enterprise Performance Pack. items.summary_html:
A critical flaw in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder can let a remote attacker run code on an affected server without signing in. The vulnerability, dubbed Java4Shell and tracked as CVE-2026-114938, can also crash the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) or expose sensitive data held in its memory.

Oracle released security updates on November 17, 2026, and the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) urged organizations to patch immediately.

The flaw sits in HotSpot, the JVM that runs Java applications in many OpenJDK distributions. That differs from Log4Shell, which affected the Log4j logging library. Updating an application’s Java libraries will not replace a vulnerable runtime. Administrators need to identify the Java build each service actually runs, including any copy shipped by the application vendor.

Security firm Calif rated Java4Shell 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, which puts it in the critical range. OpenJDK’s advisory lists a score of 8.1 under CVSS 3.1. The scores use different versions of the severity standard. Both describe a serious flaw, but neither means every Java server can be exploited. Exposure depends on the runtime, the processor, and how the application handles outside data.

Calif researcher, Quang Luong, found the flaw while examining OpenJDK HotSpot with help from an AI coding tool. The disclosure follows Calif’s work on PHP2Shell and the emergency PHP patches. Both investigations found memory flaws in shared runtimes, but the PHP flaws and Java4Shell have different causes and require separate fixes.

Base64 represents binary data as text so applications can pass it through systems that expect text. It is common in sign-in flows, file uploads, and network messages.

On supported processors, HotSpot uses a faster decoder that handles several bytes at once. A mistake in that code can make the decoder write past the end of its allocated buffer before Java rejects the bad input. Rejecting it does not undo the memory damage.

Java4Shell Exposes Java Applications

Calif reported remote code execution without a login in default test setups of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira and Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate. Its tests against Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker required authentication. The researchers also demonstrated code execution in sample applications built with Apache Struts and Spring Boot. These results describe the setups Calif tested, not every installation of those products.

The risk is not limited to servers that accept incoming requests. Calif also reported a client-side demonstration in which a Java program could be compromised after opening an encrypted TLS connection to a malicious server.

The researchers compared the memory exposure to Heartbleed because a successful attack could reveal data already held by the process, such as session tokens or private keys. The two flaws do not share the same cause.

The vulnerable decoder requires an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI support, a feature available on some Intel Xeon and newer AMD processors. ARM64 systems are not affected by this code path. The earlier Cybersecurity News report on the Java 17 flaw focused on that release line. The OpenJDK advisory now identifies fixes for Java 17, 21, 25 and 27. Oracle also lists a specific Java 8 Enterprise Performance Pack build and certain GraalVM builds as affected.

There is no single exploit that works across all Java applications, according to Calif. WatchTowr also expects attacks to be tailored to individual products because the CPU, JDK, and the way the application uses Base64 all matter. The research demonstrations establish that code execution is possible, but they are not evidence of attacks against production systems.

How to patch Java4Shell and Fix Versions

Oracle’s fixed Java SE releases include 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1. Organizations using Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Azul Zulu, or another distribution should check their vendor’s advisory for the build that fixes this CVE.

Verify the exact build in Oracle’s advisory. Oracle GraalVM for JDK 1717.0.21.0.3Install Oracle’s November 17 security update for GraalVM for JDK 17. Oracle GraalVM for JDK 2121.0.13.0.3Install Oracle’s November 17 security update for GraalVM for JDK 21. CISA recommends patching internet-facing systems first and checking for runtimes bundled with third-party software, container images, and appliances. Those copies may not appear as separate entries in a software inventory.

Where patching must wait, Calif recommends starting affected JVMs with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to turn off the optimized Base64 routines. Another option on x86-64 is -XX:UseAVX=2, which disables AVX-512. Do not add the second flag to ARM startup settings because it can prevent Java from starting.

CISA also recommends restricting unauthenticated access, validating Base64 input before it reaches the decoder, and enforcing input-size limits while teams prepare updates. These are temporary controls, not replacements for a patched runtime.

After updating, restart each affected service or redeploy it with a rebuilt container image. Verify the version used by the running process rather than checking only the host’s default Java installation.

CISA also recommends watching for unexpected JVM crashes, unapproved runtimes, and suspicious Java processes. A crash alone does not prove exploitation, but an unexplained crash on an exposed, unpatched system deserves investigation.
